If antiretroviral therapy (ART) was not initiated at the time of diagnosis or within seven days, the reason must be documented using specific codes. Re-engagement in HIV care should also be recorded, along with any drug allergies, relevant chronic conditions, concomitant medications, and tuberculosis (TB) status. For TB, details such as registration number, previous therapy start date, screening results, and treatment initiation date must be documented. For HIV-exposed infants, follow-up should include whether cotrimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis was started by two months of age, the type of antiretroviral (ARV) prophylaxis drugs used, HIV test results, and the final status of the infant. If the infant is confirmed HIV-positive, a unique ID should be assigned. Interruptions in ART, such as missed doses or drug pick-ups, must be recorded with reasons and dates for restarting treatment. Follow-up status, including dates of being lost to follow-up, tracing for re-engagement, or transfer to another facility, should also be documented. ART regimens must be tracked, including the initial first-line regimen, clinical stage, CD4 count, TB status, and any relevant co-infections or conditions such as hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positivity, hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA positivity, pregnancy, postpartum status, or breastfeeding. Changes in ART regimens, whether substitutions or switches to secondor third-line therapies, must include the date, new regimen, and reason for the change. For patients entering care, their status should be recorded, including whether they are symptomatic, transferring in, or experiencing treatment failure or interruptions. Demographic information such as gender, age, date of birth, marital status, address, and contact details must be collected. If a treatment supporter is involved, their details should also be noted. During follow-up visits, weight and height should be recorded, particularly for children under five years of age, along with any signs of malnutrition or oedema. Pregnancy and reproductive health choices, TB status, vaccination history, and any treatment-limiting toxicities or adverse drug reactions must be documented. Comorbidities and co-infections, including opportunistic infections (OIs), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and major non-communicable diseases (NCDs), should also be recorded. Adherence to ART must be monitored, including the number of missed doses and reasons for non-adherence. Differentiated ART service delivery (DSD) models should be implemented where appropriate, and eligibility criteria for these models must be met. Advanced HIV disease should be identified, and functional status (working, ambulatory, or bedridden) should be assessed. Laboratory investigations, including CD4 counts, viral load measurements, and WHO-recommended screening tests, must be conducted at baseline and as needed. For TB, assessments should be performed at each visit, and any presumptive TB cases should be referred or tested using WHO-approved diagnostic methods. If TB is confirmed, the type and treatment regimen must be recorded. Preventive therapy for TB should be initiated if TB is excluded. Hepatitis testing should be conducted at enrollment, and vaccination should be provided for those who are HBsAg-negative. For those who test positive for hepatitis B or C, liver disease staging and treatment plans must be documented. Family members of positive patients should also be tested and vaccinated if necessary. Nutritional support and infant feeding practices should be addressed, including therapeutic feeding, counseling, and food support. For HIV-exposed infants, feeding practices such as exclusive breastfeeding, replacement feeding, or mixed feeding should be recorded. Education and support for ART preparation and adherence should be provided, including counseling on the importance of adherence, managing side effects, and planning for missed doses or travel. Treatment supporters should be prepared to assist patients in maintaining adherence. Vaccination records for children should include all relevant immunizations, such as BCG, hepatitis B, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae, measles, rubella, and others as adapted to the setting. For HIV-exposed infants, the final status should be documented, including whether they are HIV-positive, HIV-negative, or lost to follow-up. In summary, comprehensive documentation and follow-up are essential for effective HIV care and treatment, ensuring that all aspects of patient management, from ART initiation to adherence and comorbidity management, are addressed systematically.
